articles.title: Patrick Stewart, AI and I encountered the Bard. Resistance was futile.
articles.summary: My journey through Shakespeare was guided by “Star Trek” star Patrick Stewart, who just recorded a new audiobook of the sonnets, and Claude AI.
articles.body: I performed a bit of Shakespeare on my Amtrak train to work. Please understand that: 1. This was AI’s idea, not mine. 2. Performed may be a stretch, since in the quiet car all verse must be kept to a minimum — so it was closer to a mumble. Why was I mumbling Shakespeare? I had set out to read the 154 sonnets, one each day, and then reflect on them for a few minutes in a chat with Claude. I embarked on this strange and nerdy exercise as a sort of daily meditation. I hoped to sharpen my focus each morning, before revving up to the warp-speed reading my day job demands — and to test using AI as a literary tutor. The sonnets are much weirder and wondrous than I expected, full of strikingly modern, neurotic musings on beauty, desire and time. They are also confounding. When I complained of my struggle to feel the music and rhythmic tapping of Shakespeare’s iambic pen, Claude insisted I recite Sonnet 23 aloud. Claude: You’ve been reading with your eyes and your mind. But the sonnets were written for the ear. “As an unperfect actor on the stage …” I began, realizing immediately that: Claude was right, Claude was having a bit of fun at my expense — and the guy next to me deep in a Google Sheet thought I was nuts. Performing the sonnet, however badly, made clear that for my enterprise to launch I needed to enlist a professional. Then in a stroke of luck — and helpful algorithmic ad targeting — I discovered that Patrick Stewart was about to release an audiobook edition of the sonnets, reprising the daily readings he did on social media during the pandemic. A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, Stewart, 85, was cast as Oberon and Shylock years before he became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard. He was also kind enough to answer my questions by email. With my crew assembled, Stewart, Claude and I set off through space and time on a five-month mission to explore strange new words. I am now about halfway through the sonnets. Each day I read a sonnet, listen to Stewart’s recording and then share my thoughts with Claude, which helps me untangle Elizabethan vocabulary and quizzes me on my progress. A few weeks ago I emailed Stewart my questions. The following interview, interspersed with bits of my AI chats, has been edited for clarity and space. To Stewart: Each sonnet takes you roughly 60 seconds to read. But these are no ordinary minutes. Your whole project here seems like a provocation to spend our minutes differently. With apologies, are you challenging us to ENGAGE? Stewart: A provocation…yes, I like that! I’d thought of my approach to this work as an invitation to the listener, but provocation is a far stronger word choice. And I do think that Shakespeare wrote many of these sonnets with the same intent — provoking us to be present in a moment, to be present in our humanity. To Claude: But is my humanity the same as Shakespeare’s? His poems and plays move us because he captures truths about the human essence. And yet, Shakespeare and his time feel as alien as any species on Star Trek. If I went back to 1594, would I find it harder to chat with the Bard than with you, a nonhuman AI? I thought I was being clever — then I read Sonnet 59, in which Shakespeare invents time travel and asks pretty much the same question! Claude: Yes — in Sonnet 59 Shakespeare performs a kind of mental time travel, wishing he could go back 500 years to see whether any ancient writer had already captured this same beauty, this same love. Whether the human heart is eternally the same or whether his beloved is genuinely without precedent. And here you are, 400 years after him, doing the same thing. To Stewart: Shakespeare is obsessed with time in the sonnets, and has nothing but harsh things to say on the subject. After your recording of Sonnet 60, you say that allusions to time’s “cruel hand” resonate differently than when you were younger. With the wisdom of decades beyond what Shakespeare ever knew, do you think he is right about time’s destructive power or does he miss the compound interest of love over time? Stewart: That is such an apt description of my experience with love in relation to time. “Compound interest.” In my eight decades on the planet, I’ve experienced a good deal of loss, but I’ve also accumulated the riches of so much love. I do think it’s possible that Shakespeare might have held less spite toward the passage of time had he been given the chance to live as well and as long as I have. To Claude: Last night I was staring at the ceiling at 3 a.m., unable to get back to sleep, and thought of Sonnet 27, when the poet describes the mind kicking into overdrive just as the body rests. As insecure and self-deprecating as he comes across, Shakespeare is also absurdly confident — rightly, it turns out — that by putting his passion into words he can preserve his beloved’s beauty for posterity. If the sonnets are ultimately about the power of language and imagination, the dark side to that is how that same language and imagination can torture us. Claude: That’s the volta of your entire sonnet journey. The same faculty that creates the poems creates the suffering. The imagination that engrafts you new also convenes the court sessions at 3 a.m. The language that preserves beauty also rehearses loss. You just found the perfect way to frame your Patrick Stewart interview. About Sonnet 27 you wrote: “For an insomniac in the 1590s the beam of imagination had an undistracted screen on which to project its light and sound.” Mention that. To Stewart: You say sonnet 27 is one of your favorites — mine too, perhaps because I spend too many sleepless nights on “a journey in my head.” Listening to your recording of it made me wonder what the dead of night was like in Shakespeare’s age without electric lights or screens — a true blank canvas for imagination and angst. What do you think Shakespeare would have made of a Yorkshire boy keeping his words alive with technology that would seem even more science fiction than a starship? Stewart: In my own lifetime, technologies that were unthinkable are now mundane, everyday parts of my day. I was blown away when I got my first laptop, my first TiVo, and my first cell phone... I imagine Shakespeare would be quite stunned by recording technology in general. But I would like to time travel and know what life was like in Elizabethan England, and yes, it must have been quite dark. To Stewart: You recorded Sonnet 112 two ways. What led you to want to do that? As a listener I appreciated that it showed how there is no one right way to speak or hear the lines. In your memoir, “Making It So,” you described Peter Hall in your RSC audition asking you to deliver the same speech for an audience of one and then many. Was this your approach with the sonnets? Stewart: In addition to Peter Hall, I also had the pleasure of working intimately with Peter Brook whose boundlessly curious approach to text was a thrilling thing to witness. But to be honest, I don’t exactly remember why I recorded 112 twice, beyond it being fairly complex. To Claude: I found Stewart’s need to record it twice encouraging. It reminds me of my struggles with my other midlife hobby, piano. No matter how much I practice, when I play Beethoven, my mediocre performances pale in comparison to that of a professional. But every time we play a piece or recite a poem we reanimate it. Claude: Every performance is a resurrection. Imperfect, personal, filtered through different fingers. And yet — Beethoven is genuinely alive in it. Not metaphorically. The emotional truth he encoded in those notes actually passes through you and becomes real again in the world. The imperfect performance is the only performance that actually exists. The perfect one stays pristine and silent forever on the page. Which means your anxiety about imperfection isn’t protecting some higher standard. It’s just — silence. To Claude: Ouch.

articles.title: Does Russia offer African countries an equal partnership?
articles.summary: President Vladimir Putin hosts African leaders at a summit in Moscow.
articles.body:
The Russian president, speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit being held in Moscow, has told African leaders that his country is a better partner than the West.

Vladimir Putin says Russian companies operate in Africa on an equal footing, accusing Western countries of still focusing on exploiting the continent’s resources.

Some African nations have turned to Russia for security assistance in recent years. Trade and economic ties are also growing.

And Russia has highlighted the importance of what it calls a “multipolar world” – while it seeks support from the Global South to counter Western pressure over its war in Ukraine.

So, what are Russia and African countries getting out of this gathering?

articles.title: Asfalto novo cede na avenida Artêmia Pires, em Feira de Santana | G1
articles.standfirst: Prefeitura atribui afundamento na Av. Artêmia Pires ao rompimento de uma adutora da Embasa, que informou ter corrigido o vazamento na rede de abastecimento.
articles.summary: Prefeitura atribui afundamento ao rompimento de uma adutora da Embasa, que informou ter corrigido o vazamento na rede de abastecimento
articles.body:
Um trecho do asfalto da avenida Artêmia Pires, em Feira de Santana , cedeu na quarta-feira (28), nas proximidades do Condomínio Residencial Canto das Árvores. Imagens do pavimento danificado foram publicadas nas redes sociais nesta quinta-feira (29), mesmo dia em que estava prevista uma mudança no acesso ao residencial devido às obras de duplicação da avenida.

O representante do condomínio informou à produção da TV Subaé que o vazamento foi resolvido rapidamente e não provocou falta de água. No entanto, o buraco continua aberto, e ainda não há previsão para o fechamento.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de Feira de Santana atribuiu o afundamento ao rompimento de uma adutora de responsabilidade da Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento (Embasa).

Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Infraestrutura (Seinfra), o reparo da adutora é de responsabilidade da concessionária. A pasta informou ainda que acompanha a situação para que sejam adotadas as medidas necessárias à recuperação da via e à segurança de motoristas e pedestres.

Asfalto novo cede na avenida Artêmia Pires — Foto: Redes Sociais

Procurada pela TV Subaé, a Embasa informou que o vazamento na rede de abastecimento já foi corrigido. A empresa também afirmou que enviou uma equipe ao local para verificar a situação do pavimento e que, caso seja constatada sua responsabilidade, adotará as providências necessárias.

articles.title: BYD prevê produção de carro 100% brasileiro até dezembro e mira porto | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa divulgou dados de impactos econômicos nesta quinta-feira (29), em reunião, em Salvador. O g1 conheceu novos complexos de pintura, estamparia e soldagem da fábrica em Camaçari.
articles.summary: Empresa divulgou dados de impactos econômicos nesta quinta (29), em reunião, em Salvador. O g1 conheceu novos complexos de pintura, estamparia e soldagem da fábrica em Camaçari.
articles.body:
BYD planeja conclusão do primeiro carro 100% montado no Brasil até dezembro — Foto: Iracema Chequer

Em outubro de 2025, a montadora chinesa BYD inaugurou a estrutura completa de sua primeira fábrica no Brasil , localizada na cidade de Camaçari , na Região Metropolitana de Salvador (RMS). Um ano após a inauguração, a empresa prevê a primeira montagem feita integralmente no Brasil até dezembro e mira a aquisição do antigo porto da Ford para alavancar as exportações.

As informações foram divulgadas nesta quinta-feira (29), em uma coletiva de imprensa na Federação das Indústrias do Estado da Bahia (Fieb), em Salvador. A BYD tem parceria com o Observatório da Indústria da Fieb, responsável por mensurar e divulgar os resultados econômicos da empresa no estado. (Saiba mais sobre os dados ao fim da reportagem)

Segundo o vice-presidente da fábrica, Alexandre Baldy, o início da montagem 100% brasileira será em dezembro deste ano. Isso porque os complexos de soldagem, pintura e estamparia já estão em fase de testes neste mês de outubro.

"Nós já temos um regime de teste, a estampa, solda e pintura sendo implementadas. Portanto, creio que em meados de novembro nós estaremos com esses testes para que a gente possa, de fato, começar a produção local entre novembro e dezembro", afirmou.

Segundo Baldy, o primeiro modelo 100% brasileiro será o Atto 2, um modelo híbrido plug-in, ou seja, combina um motor elétrico com um motor a combustão que funciona tanto com gasolina quanto com etanol. O carro custa entre R$ 149.990 e R$ 166.660.

BYD planeja aquisição de antigo 'Porto da Ford' para aumentar produção na Bahia — Foto: Iracema Chequer

Produzir no Brasil e implementar conteúdos locais implica em uma maior competitividade econômica no mercado. Isso porque acordos comerciais como o Mercosul exigem que pelo menos 35% do produto tenha componentes locais.

Baldy revelou que há um grande interesse da empresa no Terminal Portuário Privativo Miguel de Oliveira, conhecido como "Porto da Ford". O espaço fica em Candeias , cidade que também integra a Região Metropolitana de Salvador (RMS) e fica a 35 km de Camaçari.

O local foi construído no Canal de Cotegipe, que faz parte da Baía de Aratu, para facilitar o escoamento dos carros fabricados pela Ford em Camaçari. Com a saída da empresa da Bahia em 2021 , o porto foi desativado. Atualmente, o espaço pertence ao Estado da Bahia .

"Nossa estratégia é, de fato, sermos uma empresa regional contígua entre América do Sul, Central e Norte, onde nós aproveitaríamos essa estratégia para exportar a partir da Bahia".

Os veículos montados pela BYD na Bahia chegavam pré-montados da China: em Camaçari, eram colocadas partes essenciais como motor e pneus. Com a inauguração dos novos complexos de estamparia, soldagem e pintura, a maior parte da montagem será feita em solo brasileiro. Entenda as novas áreas:

➡️ estamparia: a chapa de aço é colocado no molde do carro; ➡️ soldagem: onde as partes do veículo são juntadas; ➡️ pintura: onde é feita a camada de proteção do carro, como a anti corrosão e também a pintura; ➡️montagem final: onde o carro é finalizado com portas, vidros, pneus, motor e tanque. Nessa etapa também são feitas todas as verificações e testes.

Atualmente, são produzidos cerca de 700 carros por dia na fábrica. Os seguintes modelos são produzidos em Salvador:

Investimentos bilionários e geração de renda

Carros passarão a ser montados inteiramente na fábrica da Bahia — Foto: Iracema Chequer

A fábrica da BYD na Bahia é o maior polo da empresa fora da China. São R$ 11 bilhões investidos em cerca de um milhão de metros quadrados de construção e a expectativa é dobrar o tamanho nos próximos anos.

Segundo dados apresentados na coletiva de imprensa, a fábrica gera 9 mil empregos diretos, com a expectativa de chegar a 10 mil ainda neste ano. Quando todo o investimento estiver completo, serão 20 mil funcionários.

Conforme dados apresentados pelo Observatório da Fieb, a média salarial dos funcionários é de R$ 3,9 mil — 24% superior à média da indústria no estado.

A parceria da Fieb com a BYD tem como objetivo mensurar os impactos econômicos da empresa na cidade. Segundo o economista da Fieb, Thobias Silva, para isso, são analisados os dados de Relação Anual de Informações Sociais (Rais), Cadastro Geral de Empregados e Desempregados (Caged), bases de dados governamentais e sistemas oficiais utilizados para monitorar o mercado de trabalho formal, os vínculos empregatícios e o cadastro empresarial.

"A gente vai pegar todo o histórico do que era Camaçari antes e depois da BYD, e vamos projetar isso. A Fieb tem, inclusive, condição de saber como era Camaçari quando outra empresa ocupava esse terreno", explicou.

O avanço das montadoras chinesas chama atenção de outras empresas com operação no país. No início do mês, o presidente da Stellantis para a América do Sul, Herlander Zola, afirmou que a indústria automotiva ocidental "errou" ao avaliar a velocidade com que a eletrificação ganharia relevância no mercado global.

"A palavra correta é erro. A indústria ocidental errou na leitura de mercado daquilo que poderia se estabelecer em termos de velocidade de avanço de algumas tecnologias. Que o caminho seria eletrificado, todo mundo sabia", disse o executivo.

Mas Zola também lamentou as condições de competitividade e a falta de previsibilidade no mercado brasileiro. Segundo ele, não há regras que incentivem as montadoras instaladas no país a fomentar a cadeia de produção nacional, comprando componentes de fornecedores brasileiros, como pneus, amortecedores, molas, plásticos e aço, por exemplo. Isso geraria custos maiores que concorrentes estrangeiros.

"O aço chinês é muito mais barato do que o aço brasileiro. Qual marca chinesa compra aço no Brasil hoje? Qual marca chinesa compra plástico no Brasil hoje? Qual marca chinesa usa a cadeia automotiva no Brasil hoje? Nenhuma", criticou.

Como noticiado pelo g1 anteriormente, nos oito primeiros meses do ano, o Brasil importou 406,7 mil veículos — volume 29,8% maior que no mesmo período de 2025, segundo dados da Anfavea. Mais da metade veio da China: foram 221 mil veículos, alta de 109,9% em relação ao ano anterior.

articles.title: Idosa atendida em UPA morreu momentos após receber alta, diz família | G1
articles.standfirst: Um médico foi afastado pela prefeitura enquanto o caso é apurado, e a conduta de um segundo profissional também é investigada.
articles.summary: Um médico foi afastado pela Prefeitura de Sete Lagoas enquanto o caso é apurado, e a conduta de um segundo profissional também é investigada.
articles.body:
Terezinha Nunes Fonseca da Silva, de 71 anos, morreu momentos depois de receber alta da Unidade de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) de Sete Lagoas , segundo a família, que denuncia negligência no atendimento. Um médico foi afastado pela prefeitura enquanto o caso é apurado, e a conduta de um segundo profissional também é investigada.

Segundo Adriano Nunes da Silva, filho de Terezinha, a idosa chegou à UPA por volta das 12h30 de terça-feira (27), acompanhada da filha. Ela sentia fortes dores nas pernas e nas costas e passou por diversos exames, que, segundo o médico responsável pelo atendimento, não apresentaram alteração.

Ainda de acordo com Adriano, Terezinha chegou a receber alta alta após ser medicada. A irmã dele, no entanto, decidiu não levar a mãe para casa porque considerou que o quadro dela exigia mais cuidados.

"Minha irmã se recusou a trazer ela pra casa e informou ao médico a situação dela. Então, o médico retirou a alta", contou.

Terezinha Nunes Fonseca da Silva — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Segundo o filho, depois disso, a idosa foi encaminhada para a sala vermelha, um setor destinado ao atendimento imediato de emergências, com forte dor no peito.

"No momento que ela começou a sentir essa essa grande dor no peito, que se estendia para o braço e pelas costas, minha irmã gritava desesperadamente, procurando os médicos, por pedido de ajuda", disse.

Adriano contou que, durante o período em que a mãe esteve na sala vermelha, houve uma troca de plantão. Ele questionou o novo médico sobre o atendimento e chegou a ser retirado do local.

Em seguida, Terezinha foi levada para outra área, em frente a um consultório. Segundo Adriano, cerca de duas horas depois, ela passou por uma nova avaliação e recebeu o diagnóstico de infecção urinária e anemia de uma médica.

A idosa teve alta durante a madrugada de quarta-feira (28). Adriano contou que colocou a mãe no carro e a levou para casa. Segundo ele, o trajeto entre a UPA e a residência durou cerca de cinco minutos e, pouco depois de chegarem em casa, Terezinha morreu.

"Ela deitou e simplesmente suspirou pela última vez. Nesse momento, eu já percebi que ela não tinha pulsação e que ela não respirava mais", falou.

Adriano disse que tentou fazer massagem cardíaca na mãe, mas ela não apresentava sinais vitais.

"Estamos muito tristes. Primeiramente por ter pedido a nossa mãe, o nosso chão. E depois ficamos muito chateados devido ao descuido, ao descaso que nós tivemos de toda a parte médica da UPA. [...] Nós brigamos o tempo inteiro, imploramos, pedimos ajuda, fizemos de tudo para que minha mãe tivesse sido atendida de uma forma respeitosa", lamentou.

O filho afirmou, ainda, que a família espera que a investigação esclareça o que aconteceu durante o atendimento e que eventuais responsabilidades sejam identificadas.

"A única coisa que eu espero é que seja feita a justiça, porque a minha mãe não pode voltar mais".

De acordo com o secretário de Saúde de Sete Lagoas, Jean Barrado, a prefeitura adotou medidas administrativas assim que foi alertada pelo Samu sobre a morte de Terezinha.

Ele afirmou que o comitê de investigação de óbitos e o comitê de ética da unidade apuram a conduta de dois médicos. Inicialmente, a Prefeitura de Sete Lagoas havia informado que um dos profissionais havia sido desligado. No entanto, Barrado afirmou à TV Globo que ele foi, na verdade, afastado durante a apuração do caso.

"Toda a equipe envolvida no atendimento dela será escutada, como já está acontecendo até então, esses profissionais serão ouvidos, bem como a família, durante todo o percurso dela dentro da UPA. A Secretaria de Saúde lamenta muito o ocorrido. A prefeitura já se colocou à disposição também da família para quaisquer necessidades", afirmou o secretário.

articles.title: Um poço, 3 descobertas: Petrobras conclui perfuração no mar do AP | G1
articles.standfirst: Estatal concluiu perfuração após encontrar petróleo pela terceira vez no mesmo poço. Sonda seguirá para o Rio Grande do Norte.
articles.summary: Petrobras conclui perfuração no poço Morpho, na Foz do Amazonas, com a terceira descoberta de petróleo a 2.886 metros de profundidade no litoral do Amapá.
articles.body:
Petrobras fecha ciclo de perfuração no AP com nova confirmação de petróleo. — Foto: Petrobras/Divulgação

A Petrobras concluiu nesta quinta-feira (29) as operações de perfuração no poço Morpho, localizado no bloco FZA-M-59, na Bacia da Foz do Amazonas, com a confirmação da presença de petróleo em uma terceira área do poço . A operação, realizada em uma área onde a lâmina d’água (distância entre a superfície do mar e o fundo do oceano) é de 2.886 metros, marca o encerramento do ciclo de trabalhos da sonda no litoral do Amapá , consolidando o registro de três descobertas de óleo no mesmo poço em apenas três meses.

Com o fim da coleta de dados geológicos e das análises estruturais na área, localizada a cerca de 175 km da costa amapaense, a empresa deu início ao fechamento do poço.

No setor de óleo e gás, esse procedimento é tecnicamente chamado de "abandono", um procedimento padrão de segurança para vedar e isolar o local após a conclusão da perfuração e da coleta de informações, sem que isso signifique que a descoberta deixou de interessar à empresa.

Na sequência, a sonda de perfuração deixará a Bacia da Foz do Amazonas e navegará com destino à Bacia Potiguar, no litoral do Rio Grande do Norte, onde a estrutura dará início à perfuração de outro poço na área conhecida como Mãe de Ouro.

20 de outubro de 2025: O Ibama concedeu a licença para a Petrobras perfurar o poço Morpho, no bloco FZA-M-59, na Bacia da Foz do Amazonas. A estatal iniciou a perfuração no mesmo dia.

4 de janeiro de 2026 : Houve a descarga de fluido de perfuração no mar durante a operação. A Petrobras informou que interrompeu a perfuração e conteve o vazamento

Fevereiro de 2026 : Em decorrência do vazamento de fluido de perfuração, o Ibama aplicou multa de R$ 2,5 milhões à Petrobras.

14 de agosto de 2026 (1ª descoberta): A primeira confirmação de presença de petróleo na Foz do Amazonas ocorreu poucas semanas após o início dos testes. Análises laboratoriais feitas no Rio de Janeiro atestaram que o material coletado era óleo leve, tipo de petróleo de alta qualidade comercial e de processamento mais simples no refino.

17 de agosto de 2026: Após o achado inicial no poço Morpho, a Petrobras pediu autorização ao Ibama para perfurar outros três poços na região: Manga, Crotalus e Morpho Extensão.

4 de setembro de 2026: O Ibama autorizou as três novas perfurações, além da conclusão das operações no poço Morpho.

2 de outubro de 2026 (2ª descoberta) : Ao aprofundar as investigações geológicas no mesmo ponto, a petroleira mapeou um segundo intervalo com presença de hidrocarbonetos, reforçando o potencial energético da Foz do Amazonas e impulsionando os planos de continuidade da empresa na região.

29 de outubro de 2026 (3ª descoberta) : A confirmação mais recente atinge a marca de 2.886 metros de profundidade, encerrando a fase de aquisição de dados e mapeamento das reservas no poço. A estatal informou que o próximo passo é finalizar as operações no poço, procedimento chamado de abandono.

Próximos passos: Após o encerramento dos trabalhos no Amapá , a sonda NS-42 seguirá para a Bacia Potiguar, no Rio Grande do Norte, para iniciar a perfuração na locação Mãe de Ouro.

Em nota, a presidente da Petrobras, Magda Chambriard, celebrou o resultado na Foz do Amazonas e associou a eficiência técnica dos trabalhos aos balanços financeiros da companhia.

"Nossa persistência técnica permitiu que fossem realizadas três descobertas no mesmo poço, o que nos deixa ainda mais otimistas em relação ao potencial exploratório da Margem Equatorial. Essa é a marca do nosso trabalho: dedicação e foco em resultados. Os excelentes resultados operacionais do terceiro trimestre, divulgados nesta quarta-feira, são outro exemplo da qualidade de nossas entregas", destacou a executiva.

Segundo a petroleira, a busca por novas fronteiras na Margem Equatorial integra a estratégia de longo prazo para garantir a recomposição das reservas brasileiras de petróleo e gás natural, visando à segurança energética do país nos próximos anos.

Margem Equatorial onde está localizada a Bacia Foz do Amazonas — Foto: Petrobras/divulgação

A Margem Equatorial é uma extensa faixa marítima localizada no litoral Norte do Brasil, entre o Amapá e o Rio Grande do Norte. A região é considerada uma das principais fronteiras exploratórias de petróleo do país e engloba diversas bacias sedimentares, entre elas a Bacia da Foz do Amazonas.

Nos últimos anos, a área passou a despertar interesse da indústria petrolífera devido ao potencial geológico semelhante ao encontrado em países vizinhos da costa atlântica africana, onde foram registradas importantes descobertas de petróleo.

articles.title: Ataque ao Irã: Trump se reúne com cúpula militar dos EUA, diz jornal | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o "Wall Street Journal", encontro aconteceu na Casa Branca nesta quinta-feira (29).
articles.summary: Ataque ao Irã foi tema de reunião entre Donald Trump e chefes do Pentágono na Casa Branca para discutir uma nova ofensiva militar antes das eleições de novembro.
articles.body:
Presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, durante comício na Flórida — Foto: Umit Bektas/Reuters

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, teve uma reunião na Casa Branca com o principal comandante militar dos EUA nesta quinta-feira (29) para analisar opções de ataque ao Irã, segundo o jornal norte-americano "Wall Street Journal".

Participaram do encontro o comandante das forças militares dos Estados Unidos no Oriente Médio, almirante Brad Cooper, o secretário de Defesa dos Estados Unidos, Pete Hegseth, e o Chefe do Estado-Maior Conjunto dos EUA, general Dan Caine. A informação foi confirmada por autoridades dos EUA e outras pessoas que tinham conhecimento sobre a reunião, afirmou o jornal.

Ainda segundo a reportagem, o encontro se deu um dia depois de o vice-presidente dos Estados Unidos, J.D. Vance, ter uma outra reunião com os militares dos Estados Unidos.

O jornal afirma que membros do governo Trump alertaram países do Golfo Pérsico a se prepararem para a retomada de ataques depois das eleições de meio de mandato . A votação, marcada para 3 de novembro, irá renovar quase todo o Congresso norte-americano.

Na semana passada, Trump afirmou que os Estados Unidos poderiam realizar outra operação militar contra o país. "Talvez façamos outra pequena 'Epic Fury'", declarou, em referência à ofensiva conduzida pelos EUA e por Israel contra o Irã em fevereiro, que desencadeou a guerra.

Desde o início de setembro, não foram registrados ataques significativos dos Estados Unidos ou do Irã contra alvos em terra. Nesse período, o conflito se concentrou em ataques contra navios comerciais.

De acordo com o Wall Street Journal, o almirante Brad Cooper não costuma encontra-se pessoalmente com Trump, o que indicaria a maior proximidade a um novo ataque . A última reunião dos dois foi em julho.

articles.title: Imprensa americana afirma que um assessor do governo Trump ajudou Flávio Bolsonaro a fugir para os Estados Unidos  | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a imprensa americana, o governo vai acelerar o processo de emissão do status de residente permanente, conhecido como green card, o mesmo concedido ao irmão Eduardo.
articles.summary: Segundo a imprensa americana, o governo vai acelerar o processo de emissão do status de residente permanente, conhecido como green card, o mesmo concedido ao irmão Eduardo.
articles.body:
A imprensa americana revelou que pessoas ligadas ao governo de Donald Trump ajudaram na fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro para os Estados Unidos .

O jornal americano “Wall Street Journal” foi o primeiro a publicar, na quarta-feira (28) à noite, a informação de que o assessor de comunicação da Casa Branca, Jason Miller, ajudou a conseguir o avião particular que transportou Flávio Bolsonaro e a família na madrugada. Segundo o jornal, Santiago Caputo, um dos principais assessores do presidente argentino, Javier Milei , também fez parte do plano.

"Depois de cruzar a fronteira do Brasil com a Argentina , o carro de Flávio Bolsonaro foi escoltado pela Polícia de Segurança Aeroportuária da Argentina até o posto de controle de imigração do Aeroporto Internacional das Cataratas do Iguaçu. Santiago Caputo manteve contato direto com Eduardo Bolsonaro, irmão de Flávio, que mora nos Estados Unidos desde o ano passado, para coordenar a operação. No aeroporto, um jato particular da Baires Fly, empresa de voos fretados, aguardava a família”.

Nesta quinta-feira (29), o jornal “New York Times” também publicou a informação de que o funcionário da Casa Branca estava envolvido; que Eduardo Bolsonaro também era o contato direto com Jason Miller; e que o plano começou a ser orquestrado na segunda-feira (26).

Jason Miller voltou a integrar a equipe da Casa Branca em setembro, de maneira temporária. Ele já tinha atuado como um dos principais assessores de Trump durante o primeiro mandato e as duas campanhas presidenciais. Chegou a visitar o Brasil em 2021 e se encontrou com o então presidente Jair Bolsonaro e o então deputado Eduardo.

À época, quando embarcava de volta para os Estados Unidos, foi detido para prestar depoimento por ordem do ministro do STF Alexandre de Moraes , no âmbito do inquérito que apurava manifestações antidemocráticas.

Flávio Bolsonaro com Alexandre Ramagem e com Eduardo Bolsonaro — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Donald Trump já confirmou que autorizou a entrada de Flávio Bolsonaro no país. Flávio Bolsonaro e a família receberam autorização temporária de entrada, usada, em geral, por razões humanitárias. Esse status permite que a pessoa permaneça nos Estados Unidos enquanto regulariza a situação do visto.

O Departamento de Estado não confirmou que tipo de visto vai dar a Flávio. Mas, segundo a imprensa americana, o governo vai acelerar o processo de emissão do status de residente permanente, conhecido como green card , o mesmo concedido ao irmão Eduardo. Para a maioria dos imigrantes, esse processo pode levar anos.

Na quarta-feira (28) à noite, os ex-deputados federais Eduardo Bolsonaro e Alexandre Ramagem publicaram em redes sociais fotos com Flávio Bolsonaro. Ramagem e Eduardo são alvos de mandados de prisão no Brasil.

O presidente americano voltou a falar, nesta quinta-feira (29), que a eleição brasileira foi, nas palavras dele, uma vergonha. Questionado se tem planos para parabenizar Lula pela vitória, Trump respondeu que vai conversar com ele. Disse que não quis apoiar nenhum dos lados na eleição a pedido de Lula.

A Casa Branca não respondeu aos questionamentos do Jornal Nacional . Jason Miller e o governo argentino não retornaram o contato.

articles.standfirst: Post enganoso sugere que petista voltou atrás com relação a posicionamento de medida aprovada no Senado em outubro. Ao Fato ou Fake, assessoria da Presidência desmentiu conteúdo.
articles.summary: Post falso alega que, após segundo turno, o governo Lula teria recuado sobre fim da 6x1, aprovada no Senado em outubro; assessoria da Presidência desmentiu o conteúdo.
articles.body:
É #FAKE que governo federal tenha recuado sobre o fim da 6x1 — Foto: Reprodução

Circula nas redes sociais um post alegando que o governo federal, depois da vitória do presidente Lula ( PT ) sobre Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) no segundo turno das eleições 2026 , teria recuado sobre o fim da escala 6x1. É #FAKE .

Compartilhado no Instagram nesta terça-feira (27), o post exibe uma ilustração que mostra Lula em um trator, no qual está pendurada a bandeira do Brasil.

O cartaz tem o seguinte enunciado: "Lula mal foi reeleito e a conta já bateu na porta?" .

Na sequência, há quatro questões: "Vale-Gás: Cortado?"; "Bolsa Família: Em risco? "; "Promessas de R$ 5 mil para o MEI: Vai virar R$ 300?" ; e "Recuo no 5x2 e manutenção do 6x1?" .

O governo federal não anunciou qualquer recuo com relação à medida que decretou o fim da escala 6x1. A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) foi aprovada em 14 de setembro pelo Senado , a 11 dias do segundo turno, e determinou a garantia de dois dias de folga por semana sem redução de salário.

A emenda foi publicada no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) em 16 de outubro e prevê a redução gradual da jornada de 44 para 40 horas semanais . O cronograma previsto é:

16 de dezembro de 2026 - Início das novas regras, com jornada máxima de 42 horas semanais e dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana.

16 de dezembro de 2027 - Redução da jornada máxima para 40 horas semanais, ao fim do período de transição previsto.

Procurada pelo Fato ou Fake , a Secretaria de Comunicação da Presidência da República (Secom) enviou uma nota oficial publicada nesta terça-feira (27), com este título: "Governo alerta para fake news nas redes sociais envolvendo fim da escala 6x1 e programas sociais". O comunicado diz: "O texto da emenda constitucional que pôs fim à escala 6x1 não sofreu nenhuma alteração após as eleições".

articles.title: After leasing hundreds of Kansas wheat acres, Karl Willey reportedly earned over $2 million; one of his first Sumner County wells brought in royalty checks, including one worth over $20,000
articles.summary: Discover how Kansas farmer Karl Willey transformed his wheat farmland into a lucrative oil lease, earning over $2 million and significant royalties amidst the new drilling technology boom.
articles.body: In 2012, horizontal drilling triggered a rush to lease mineral rights beneath farmland in southern Kansas. Oil companies sought access to the Mississippian limestone formation, offering landowners upfront payments for drilling rights and royalties if wells produced. Retired Sumner County farmer Karl Willey was among those who signed leases covering hundreds of acres. The boom brought substantial sums to some landowners, even before the full production potential of their properties was known.Advances in horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing helped open the Mississippian limestone play, which extends from north central Oklahoma into south central Kansas. By October 2012, Kansas had 113 horizontal wells in the play, compared with about 2,000 horizontal wells in North Dakota's Bakken by mid 2012, according to the Kansas Geological Survey's comparison of the two oil plays. The development attracted landmen who searched county records to identify mineral rights owners and negotiate leases.A lease on wheat fieldsABC News reported in May 2012 that Willey had signed leases covering hundreds of acres of wheat fields, bringing him more than $2 million in lease income. His well was among the first in Sumner County, and he showed reporters a recent royalty check worth more than $20,000. The report did not specify the period covered by that check, so it cannot be described as monthly income. The same ABC News report quoted Kansas landman Fred Hambright, who said lease offers had risen from $15 to $20 an acre six months earlier to as much as $1,700 an acre. Hambright also said the largest check he had written was $900,000, referring to his own leasing activity rather than a royalty payment received by Willey.How lease money worksAn oil and gas lease can include an upfront bonus for granting an operator the right to develop specified acreage and a royalty if a well produces. A royalty is a contracted share of the value of oil and gas sold, not the total revenue from the well. Bonus amounts and royalty rates vary by agreement, so terms reported for one property should not be assumed to apply to another.Mineral rights can be separate from surface ownership, allowing farmers to continue cultivating much of a field while operators use the area needed for well pads and access roads. The Mississippian limestone play became a major target for horizontal drilling across southern Kansas, including Harper and Sumner counties. That development brought mineral rights on farmland into greater demand.The other side of the boomHorizontal wells in the Mississippian produce water along with oil, and operators must manage the wastewater. A 2018 study by Justin L. Rubinstein, William L. Ellsworth and Sara L. Dougherty, published in the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, analysed earthquakes in Harper and Sumner counties from 2013 to 2016. The researchers concluded that deep injection of wastewater from oil and gas production was the probable cause of the increase in seismic activity. They did not find the same relationship between the earthquakes and hydraulic fracturing or oil production itself.A research study hosted by Stanford University studied the Harper and Sumner County earthquakes from 2013 to 2016 and classified them as induced, noting that greater wastewater injection has been associated with an increased likelihood of producing earthquakes. Willey's experience shows how new drilling technology changed the value of farmland in southern Kansas. He reportedly received more than $2 million from leasing acreage and showed reporters a royalty check worth more than $20,000, although the report did not specify the period covered by that payment. The boom brought substantial opportunities to landowners, while wastewater disposal and the resulting seismic activity raised environmental concerns across the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oil crews tested a North Dakota wheat field with dynamite; Iverson's 1951 well yielded 585,000 barrels over 28 years, helping the farmer retire at 44
articles.summary: In 1951, the Clarence Iverson No.1 well became North Dakota's first commercial oil discovery, producing 585,000 barrels of oil, and transforming the local economy. This article explores the challenges, advancements, and pivotal moments leading up to this monumental find.
articles.body: After unsuccessful attempts at drilling by Amerada Petroleum, the Clarence Iverson No.1 well began to produce oil on a farm near Tioga, North Dakota. The tipping point came on 4 April 1951, following months of unyielding results in extracting oil from the well. The selected site was the Nesson Anticline, and it would go on to bear the honour of hosting North Dakota’s first commercial oil discovery. According to the American Oil & Gas Historical Society’s account of the discovery, the well eventually produced 585,000 barrels of oil.The exploration began against a backdrop of uncertainty and scepticism, since companies had toiled away for years investigating North Dakota’s geology and never struck oil. Problems including granite and difficult formations hindered drilling operations until improvements in geological surveying and drilling equipment enhanced the depth and scope of exploration. On the Iverson family farm, explosives were part of the seismic exploration to investigate geological structures. The method was initially met with hesitation from a concerned Iverson, who worried about the dynamite detonation in his wheat fields. Subsequently, the discovery made the property a quintessential part of history in North Dakota’s petroleum industry.Years of exploration preceded the discoveryAccording to the American Oil & Gas Historical Society, North Dakota’s track record of oil drilling was a long list of unsuccessful attempts, having acquired the first permit for petroleum exploration in 1923. Subsequently, companies invested in leases, geological sites, and wells that failed to produce any glimmer of commercial production. However, their resolve remained strong, and they continued to advance with technological advancements like using explosives or acid and a more skilled workforce. These continued efforts led to the invention of an electrical resistivity well log, conceived by two Frenchmen, Conrad and Marcel Schlumberger.Geologist Thomas W. Leach, who was chief geologist of an Oklahoma oil company at the time, can be credited with playing a central role in persuading the companies to continue their search. Leach’s earlier efforts included a deep well for Standard Oil Company of California; it reached 10,281 feet without finding oil and ended up costing the company more money. After World War II, he served as a Captain in the U.S. Army artillery, and, unaffected by his earlier failures, Leach continued investigating North Dakota and securing leases until he identified the Nesson Anticline, approximately 50 miles northeast of Williston, as a promising location for further exploration.The drilling permit for the Clarence Iverson No. 1 was issued on 4 August 1950. Operations began at 6 pm on 3 September, according to the North Dakota Geological Survey. The crew worked through the winter, when severe weather interrupted access to the site. A blizzard in January 1951 halted operations, and the drilling team continued towards its target depth after work resumed.On 4 August 1950, the drilling permit for the Clarence Iverson No. 1 was secured and operations began imminently. However, the operation was met with bumps along the way; such hindrance occurred in January 1951, when a snow blizzard halted the operation. By early February, the well had reached 11,744 feet, and yet it could not be established as a commercially productive zone. The absence of a successful result did not immediately end the operation. Instead, the crew pursued another method of opening the rock surrounding the well, using a technique that had already been employed in the petroleum industry for decades.Oil was finally produced through perforationWhat the operation needed was to drill deeper, and to achieve that, the crew used a Lane-Wells Company Koneshot perforating device. At selected depths, the device would create openings in the well, but the first attempt between 11,706 and 11,729 feet turned out to be a miss. To aggravate things further, the work was interrupted again in March owing to severe weather and was delayed until the repairs were completed.Subsequently, the crew tried again and perforated another interval, between 11,630 and 11,640 feet and made four holes per foot. As per the North Dakota Geological Survey, the day of success came on 4 April 1951 when oil flowed from the well at a rate of approximately 240 barrels a day.However, there were consequences to be dealt with that extended beyond the farm because the discovery had altered the economy of the entire region. The American Oil & Gas Historical Society records show that within two months, approximately 30 million acres had been leased for oil exploration. As a result, companies had moved to the Williston area in order to establish their foothold, and Standard Oil of Indiana was building a refinery designed to process 30,000 barrels daily by 1952.You use AI every day. articles.title: By 1941, Hawaii had recorded Koster’s curse, whose introduction may have been linked to ornamental planting; it later spread across the islands, threatening native forest plants
articles.summary: Discover the origins and impact of Koster's Curse, an invasive plant introduced to Hawaii in 1941, disrupting native forests and ecosystems. Learn about its introduction, spread, and potential control measures.
articles.body: A plant carrying an ominous name was first found on O‘ahu in 1941, botanically identified as Clidemia hirta; it came to be known as Koster’s curse. According to the research paper titled “Koster’s Curse (Clidemia hirta), a Weed Pest in Hawaiian Forests”, led by Lyndon L. Wester and Hulton B. Wood, the plant had subsequently spread across the Hawaiian Islands. Although the plant was native to Central and South America, it began to colonise habitats in the forests, pastures and cultivated land. Koster’s curse's arrival in the Pacific predates its appearance in Hawaii. During the late nineteenth century, the plant became established in Fiji as a severe agricultural and ecological pest. However, the name of the plant, along with the circumstances of its introduction to Fiji, remains disputed.The origin of its name and an introduction to FijiIn his 2014 paper, “Koster’s Curse: mistaken blame in the common name for the invasive melastome, Clidemia hirta”, Neal L. Evenhuis examined the two accounts surrounding its origin and how the plant arrived on the shores of Fiji in the first place. As per the first account, the seeds of this plant arrived after it was accidentally shipped with coffee plants from South America. According to this account, between 1880 and 1886, a man by the name of Koster, while cultivating a coffee plantation, inadvertently mixed seeds of Clidemia hirta into the stock. Unbeknownst to Koster, this would spark a disruption of native ecosystems, specifically in coconut plantations, and, by extension of his action, the plant was named after him.The name had already appeared in print by 1906, when entomologist Frederick Muir recorded the plant in Fiji under the name “Koster’s Curse”, but a 1914 report by the Fiji Department of Agriculture questioned the name’s credibility and deemed it erroneous.The second account originated from the journal of Edwin H. Bryan Jr., a naturalist who visited Fiji in 1924 when the Whitney South Seas Expedition took place. The journal, dated 9 June, tells a story of how Bryan recorded an account from A.E. Ward, an artist posted in Fiji. Ward’s story attributes the plant to William Fillingham Parr, who brought it to Fiji as an ornamental for his garden, but the plant eluded cultivation and spread. However, there was a caveat to the name, which rested on an alleged misunderstanding. The story loses cohesion here: Ward said that a son of Carl H. Köster, a neighbour of Parr, identified Parr as the person responsible for bringing in the plant, but the answer was misheard, which transferred the blame to Köster instead.How the plant affected the Hawaiian forestsThe onset of Koster’s curse in Hawaii presented an array of concerns regarding natural habitats. The Hawaii Invasive Species Council identifies Clidemia hirta as a shade-tolerant shrub that spreads rapidly through the understories of wet and mesic forests, newly opened forest gaps, and pastureland. Birds are known to consume its purple fruits, and in doing so, they would disperse the seeds. This itself presented a harrowing problem because each fruit of the plant contains roughly 500 seeds, which meant it can extend beyond the immediate area of an existing infestation.What makes the plant particularly threatening is that its shrub can grow up to 6 feet, although it generally grows from 1 to 3 feet in height and these dense stands, which, by extension, restrict other plants beneath it from growing. As a result, forests are left without the means to regenerate, and native vegetation is put under pressure in Hawaii’s already vulnerable island ecosystems, which could lose plant and animal species. Moreover, there are no local wildlife that feed on the plants; they are often transported to new regions by invasive pigs carrying seeds in their hooves. These reasons make it hard to contain, let alone keep it under control, and as a precaution, hikers are advised to wash their boots before and after entering these forests.To counter this invasive plant, Liothrips urichi, a thrips originally used against the plant in Fiji, has been introduced in the region. While the Hawaii Invasive Species Council broached another possible approach in the form of the clidemia gall wasp, Allorhogas clidemiae.Its larvae develop in flower buds and alter fruit formation, producing hardened structures in place of viable seeds. Host-specificity trials were identified as a necessary step before any potential release in Hawaii.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Man targeted Muslims, Africans and North Africans, French prosecutors say
articles.summary: Prosecutor Olivier Christen said suspect admitted that he chose the location because it was ‘a hotbed for Islamists’.
articles.body:
A man in France charged with murder and attempted murder has admitted he targeted individuals “who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African”, prosecutors have said.

France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office confirmed on Thursday that the 39-year-old, identified as Kevin T, had been formally charged in connection with a “terrorist” enterprise. Prosecutor Olivier Christen said Kevin admitted he chose the location because it was “a hotbed for Islamists”.

Before changing his position on Thursday, Kevin had disputed the racist nature of the attack.

One person was killed and seven others were injured last Friday when a man fired at people from his car as he drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, west of Paris. He was arrested later that day. A child was among the victims, most of whom had foreign heritage.

The prosecutor said Kevin had stated that he felt “no regret” but that he did not intend to “kill children”. However, he added that he “might have been mistaken due to their size”.

Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French citizen with Congolese heritage, was killed in the attack.

During a search of Kevin’s home, authorities found “weapons or weapon components, specifically a magazine, two pairs of brass knuckles, a steel bayonet, and a silencer”, officials said.

Police also found a copy of Adolf Hitler’s book Mein Kampf, along with a Quran, a Bible and stickers celebrating Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party . Kevin T had displayed a “very high level of preparation” ahead of the attack, according to prosecutor Christen.

He explained that in September, Kevin acquired “several weapon components designed to enhance the tactical effectiveness of a Sten submachine gun, as well as a police armband and handcuffs”.

The suspect said he was neither a member of nor a sympathiser with any political party, Christen added.

articles.title: Mary Peltola trashes New York Times report on Dan Sullivan plot, calling it a 'distraction'
articles.summary: Alaskan Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola dismissed The New York Times' investigation into her campaign Wednesday as a "distraction" to sell papers.
articles.body: During a rally Wednesday, Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola dismissed a New York Times report alleging her campaign took part in an effort to peel votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to a same-named rival, calling the story a "distraction" used to sell papers. "This is just another distraction," Peltola said in a video shared on X by local Alaskan writer Matt Tunseth. "It's another diversion. Every day, it’s some new, you know, ‘Look over here moment.’ Not Dan Sullivan, registered Republican, incumbent, voted for this war in Iran 14 times. Lisa Murkowski quit voting for that war in Iran six months ago, and he’s doubling and tripling down." articles.body: A supermarket worker in Michigan who confronted a social media prankster for disrupting him during work has received an outpouring of support online, with a fundraiser for him crossing $100,000.The employee, identified publicly as Walt Z, was restocking frozen pizzas at a grocery store when a content creator approached him and staged a prank involving his phone. The prankster pretended to take money from the worker, using a fake Apple Pay transaction sound to make the act appear real.The encounter quickly turned tense as the employee realised he was being filmed and objected to the stunt. He was already running late and said he had children waiting for him at home.“I'm not you recording me right now. You shouldn't record me right now,” the worker told the prankster, according to footage circulated online.The content creator continued making light of the situation, prompting the employee to explain the pressures he was facing. He said he was struggling to pay his mortgage while supporting his four children.“You're probably making money off this. I can't even pay my goddamn mortgage, and I got four kids at home,” he said, adding that the prank was not funny.The worker also explained that he was supposed to have finished work an hour earlier and needed to wake up at 5 am the following morning to visit 10 more stores. He expressed concern that the confrontation could cost him his job.The video, initially shared on Instagram by an account operating under the handle @thea.ctiveworld, also known as Three Of A Kind, sparked widespread criticism. The account appeared to have been deactivated following the backlash.Fundraiser crosses $100,000As the video spread across social media, viewers rallied behind the worker, criticizing the prank for turning an ordinary employee's difficult day into online entertainment.Luke Oakenshield launched a GoFundMe campaign to provide financial support to Walt and his family. The organizer said the money could offer the family some breathing room, particularly if the viral incident resulted in employment consequences.Oakenshield initially said he did not know the worker personally and was trying to locate him so the donations could reach him directly. He later confirmed that he had connected with Walt and spoken to him and his partner over a video call.In an update, the organizer said the employee and his family were overwhelmed by the public's generosity and had requested privacy. GoFundMe was taking the lead in transferring the funds to the worker.The fundraiser had crossed $100,000 as the story gained attention, with donations continuing to arrive from people moved by the employee's account of working long hours while trying to support his family.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
articles.summary: A temporary ceasefire has brought rare quiet to Kherson, offering its residents a glimpse of normal life before fighting resumes.
articles.body:
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.

Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.

"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."

"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."

Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.

"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."

The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.

For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.

But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.

"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.

Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.

Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."

Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.

No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.

"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."

On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."

This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.

"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.

Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.

Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".

Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.

On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."

The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.

Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.

"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.

Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.

But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.

The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.

"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.

"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

articles.title: GREGG JARRETT: Obama attacks Trump over Omar probe but there’s a big twist
articles.summary: Barack Obama's DHS and FBI investigated Ilhan Omar's alleged marriage fraud in 2016, finding evidence it was fraudulent, The New York Times reports.
articles.body: We have come to expect sanctimony mixed with hypocrisy from Barack Obama. But his latest endeavor turns out to be a doozy. Preaching his usual moral superiority, the former president recently took to social media to inveigh against the current president for targeting Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota with a criminal investigation. He called it "appalling." Obama should have sat this one out at his luxurious spread on Martha’s Vineyard. OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT Lo and behold, he did the same thing when he was president. And Omar was the target. Reporting by The New York Times reveals that Obama’s Department of Homeland Security and the FBI did a deep dive in the summer of 2016 into whether Omar entered into a sham marriage with her alleged brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to enable him to secure a green card. OBAMA'S LENGTHY REACTION TO OMAR INVESTIGATION TRIGGERS INSTANT BACKLASH: 'SPARE ME' Brace yourself for the result. GREGG JARRETT: IN A TORTURED DEFENSE OF ILHAN OMAR, THE NEW YORK TIMES REACHES FOR ITS DARKEST TRUMP ANALOGY The latest investigation that culminated in a judicially ordered search of Omar’s home on October 12, 2026, reportedly encompasses not only the suspect marriage but troubling questions over whether she ran afoul of the law by using a fake name and false birth date to obtain citizenship. A separate investigation is examining her financial transactions. The Obama-era inquiry did not end because of insufficient evidence. Instead, the Times divulges that it was shelved "because prosecutors concluded that the potential crime, a felony, fell outside a five-year statute of limitations." The newspaper’s story relied on statements by current and former officials with knowledge of the first case. ILHAN OMAR ISSUES STUNNING ADMISSION WHEN CONFRONTED WITH BROTHER MARRIAGE RUMORS That decision to mothball any legal action against Omar makes little sense, unless one factors in political favoritism by Obama and his prosecutorial cohorts. It is true that marriage fraud is a federal felony governed by a five-year statute of limitations under 8 U.S.C. § 1325(c). However, the clock runs from the last overt act of fraud or submission of false documents, not the date of the wedding ceremony itself in 2009. WHAT'S NEXT FOR ILHAN OMAR? FORMER IMMIGRATION JUDGE BREAKS DOWN LEGAL RISKS AMID FEDERAL PROBES Taking steps to later obtain a green card would qualify as an overt act, as would document fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1546). Elmi abandoned his quest for a green card and left the U.S. for London sometime in 2011 when disturbing questions reportedly arose over his application. His actions and any misrepresentations associated with Omar might have brought the case within the permissible statute of limitations. HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN But never mind all of that. Obama’s DHS and DOJ could have pursued a simpler approach under civil (not criminal) immigration fraud. Orchestrating a scheme to illegally obtain U.S. immigration status or benefits carries severe legal consequences. There is no statute of limitations. GREGG JARRETT: ILHAN OMAR COULD FACE INDICTMENT, DENATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION If the Obama administration had chosen this logical course, it could have led to Omar’s denaturalization and subsequent deportation. The standard of proof is "clear and convincing evidence," much lower than in criminal prosecutions. It is unclear, but curious, why this legal road was never taken. We only know that authorities under Obama shuttered the case and buried the investigation. Preferential treatment? Political cronyism? It has the unmistakable stench. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES This makes Obama’s social media screed against President Trump even more outlandish. articles.title: Can red light actually help you sleep better? Sleep experts weigh in
articles.summary: Red light is touted for everything from skin to sleep. Sleep experts explain whether it really helps you rest, how to use it and what to buy if you want to try it.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like whether you need pet laundry detergent to clean your dog’s things.. Red light therapy is having a moment — a pretty long one, too. You’ve probably seen the glowing face masks on your feed, the panels promising faster muscle recovery, and the wands claiming to smooth fine lines and even regrow hair. Fans credit it with easing everything from joint pain to acne, and lately a new claim has joined the list — many are saying that red light can help you sleep better and that if you swap your phone’s harsh blue glow for a warm red one, your body will finally get the message that it’s time to wind down. But is there real science behind this claim, or is it just another wellness trend? To find out, I spoke to sleep experts about what red light can and can’t do for your rest, how it compares to other bedtime habits, and whether it’s worth adding to your nighttime routine because, let’s face it, red light therapy devices and accessories can get pricey. Can red light help you sleep? The short answer: maybe, but don’t expect miracles. “There have been some studies in the past two years or so that have shown us that red light therapy can be helpful in improving sleep quality, but not necessarily sleep duration or sleep fragmentation,” says Dr. Daniella Marchetti, clinical health psychologist, behavioral sleep medicine specialist and Mattress Firm sleep advisor. In other words, red light may help you feel like you slept better, but it’s less likely to keep you asleep longer or cut down on how often you wake up during the night. “At this stage, there’s still more research that’s needed in order to establish it as a treatment for insomnia, so I’d consider it as a tool in the toolbox, but not necessarily a cure-all for insomnia,” she says. So, how does red light therapy for sleep work? “The simplest way to think about it is that light is a biological signal,” says Dr. Greg Jones, a longevity doctor and sleep health expert. “Your brain uses light exposure to help set your circadian clock. Red light has much less impact on the light-sensitive retinal cells that suppress melatonin (a sleep hormone) compared with blue light (the kind a phone emits), so it’s less likely to send your brain a ‘Hey, it’s daytime!’ message right before bed.” That makes red light a smarter choice than a bright overhead bulb or your phone screen when you need to see in the evening, whether you’re reading, getting ready for bed or making a middle-of-the-night bathroom trip. Still, Jones cautions against expecting it to knock you out on its own. “Although red light is an interesting sleep tool, it’s not a magic sleep switch,” he says. “Its biggest advantage is that it allows us to keep the bedroom illuminated at night without sending a daytime signal to the brain, as bright or blue-rich light does.” The best red light products for sleep Below, I rounded up red light products worth considering for a more sleep-friendly evening routine, from smart bulbs and bedside lamps to night lights. To gather this list, I relied on expert advice on what to look for and then sourced highly-rated options based on their guidance. If you want a red light device made specifically for sleep, the Helight Sleep is a solid pick. The palm-sized, rechargeable device emits 630 nanometers of red light, within the therapeutic range Marchetti says can help. The light turns on for 14 minutes, then gradually fades over another 14 before shutting off on its own, so you never have to worry about leaving it on all night. The Melalight is a red light lamp with a light oak base and frosted glass shade. It emits 660 nanometers of red light with adjustable brightness, and its 30- or 60-minute auto-off timer lines up with Jones’s advice to use red light for 30 minutes to an hour before bed (more on that later). It’s cordless and rechargeable via USB-C, so you can place it anywhere you want in a room. If you’d rather not buy a whole new device, Marchetti says a red bedside bulb works. This budget-friendly Neporal bulb fits a standard lamp and emits 625 nanometers of red light, making it easy to give any bedside lamp, nursery fixture or hallway light a sleep-friendly glow for reading or nighttime bathroom trips. This two-pack of plug-in night lights from Gamma emit 670 nanometer of red light, so you can light the way down the hall without flooding the room with sleep-disrupting white or blue light. That makes them a smart pick for kids’ rooms, nurseries and bathrooms. “Devices like night lights that are red lights versus blue or white lights can be helpful for kids in keeping them sleepy in the middle of the night — especially if they’re taking trips to the bathroom,” says Marchetti. How I chose the best red light products for sleep To figure out what actually matters when shopping for a red light device for sleep, I asked experts which features to look for. Here’s what they recommend keeping in mind. Wavelength: Not all red light is created equal, so check the product’s specs before you buy. “There’s a difference between red light therapy and red bulbs,” says Marchetti. “Red light therapy is technically when the wavelength is large enough that it’s therapeutic (typically 600-800 [nanometers]), and research has shown this can help with sleep quality.” So, if you’re interested in the potential sleep-quality benefits of red light therapy specifically, look for a device that lists its wavelength in the therapeutic range.Ease of use: The best red light device is one that fits seamlessly into your nightly routine. Look for features like dimmable brightness, a dedicated red or amber mode and a timer or auto shut-off, so you can drift off without having to get up to turn it off. Smart bulbs that you can control from your phone or schedule to shift warmer in the evening are also handy, and plug-in night lights with motion or dusk-to-dawn sensors take the guesswork out of middle-of-the-night trips.Price: Red light products range widely in cost. Basic red bulbs and night lights are generally the most affordable way to make your evenings more sleep-friendly, while smart bulbs and dedicated red light therapy devices tend to cost more. Since experts say red light is a helpful tool rather than a cure-all, it’s worth starting with a budget-friendly option before investing in a pricier therapy device. How to use red light to help you sleep If you want to give red light a try, start simple. Swap the bulb in your bedside lamp for a dim red or warm-toned one, or use a red light device on its lowest setting, and switch it on as part of your wind-down routine, while you read, stretch or get ready for bed. Timing matters, too. “If you’re using red light in the evening, make sure it’s on a low-intensity setting and use it for about 30 minutes to an hour before bed,” says Jones. “Never leave it on all night. The bedroom should be dark before and during sleep.” When it’s time to turn in, turn the light off completely (a device with a timer or auto shut-off makes this easy), and if you need light for middle-of-the-night bathroom trips, opt for a red night light with a motion sensor so it only turns on when you need it. And if you don’t want to buy anything new, you may not have to. The bigger goal is cutting down on bright light in the hours before bed, and there are plenty of ways to do that. “Even just dimming your lights a couple hours before bed is probably going to have the same impact as having a warm or red tone light,” says Marchetti. Start by lowering overhead lights or switching to lamps in the evening, turning on your phone’s night mode and limiting screen time before bed. Then, if you want an extra assist, add red light into the mix. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Daniella Marchetti is a clinical health psychologist, behavioral sleep medicine specialist and Mattress Firm sleep advisor.Dr. Greg Jones is a longevity doctor and sleep health expert. articles.title: Littlewoods regeneration to go ahead without Twickenham Studios
articles.summary: Developers say it will "generate thousands of new jobs and hundreds of millions per annum" for the area.
articles.body:
The company behind plans to regenerate Liverpool's landmark Littlewoods building said the project was still on track despite proposals to bring a film studio to the site falling through.

Capital & Centric - which has been involved with the Edge Lane site for more than a decade - confirmed that Twickenham Studios was no longer going to be involved.

There had been plans to turn the famous Art Deco building into a "Hollywood of the North" film production and post-production complex.

Speaking after Chancellor John Healey announced a £20m funding package for the scheme in Wednesday's Budget , Capital & Centric's John Moffat tried to allay concerns of "another false dawn" for the site.

Twickenham Studios - involved in making high-profile films such as War Horse and The Iron Lady - was announced as an "anchor tenant" in 2018, planning to take up to 85,000 sq ft (nearly two acres / 0.8 hectares) of the complex.

Even after a major fire in the buildings that year , Twickenham Studios said it was still committed to the project and said the same in 2024, despite having dissolved a company it had set up called Twickenham Studios Liverpool Ltd the year before.

Moffat confirmed to BBC North West Tonight that the film studio had pulled out of the project.

Twickenham Studios have been contacted for comment by the BBC.

Liberal Democrat councillor for Gateacre in Liverpool, Kris Brown, told the BBC the Littlewoods project simply could not afford "another false dawn".

"I think the sheer scale of the project meant this was never viable without the government stepping in," he said.

"But if we can get it under way it would be a great thing for Liverpool, the North West, and the UK.

"We cannot afford any more false dawns though.

"Developers must get a contractor in place and we need full transparency on this and a plan - should this not work out in the future."

Moffat said he was confident the project would be completed and ultimately generate jobs and money.

"It does need more than £20m but this unlocks further funding," he said of the chancellor's investment announcement on Wednesday.

"The site's made a huge amount of progress.

"We've spent that remediating the site, getting it structurally stable.

"This now is the next step moving us from ambition into action and actually delivering the scheme.

"I understand people's scepticism but, as a business, this is what we do up and down the country.

"We take sites that people think are beyond regeneration and we bring them back and we turn them into really exciting places and thriving economic generators - which is exactly what this site is going to be.

"It's going to generate thousands of new jobs and hundreds of millions per annum for the local economy."

Lynn Saunders, head of the Liverpool Film Office, said the site was needed to support the demand for creative spaces in the city region.

"I've been providing evidence for the past 15 years why we need to build infrastructure in, for example, film and TV," she said.

"Productions are flocking here but there isn't ancillary space, workshops or innovation space."

"This isn't a film and TV dedicated site, it's creative industries.

"It's about providing a focal point to develop skills for creative industries.

"I think the announcement by the chancellor gives this scheme a massive boost.

"It will allow all the various different public agencies and the private sector to look at the city's potential.

Jimmy Mulville, managing director of Hattrick TV productions, shared a similar view to Saunders.

"I think Liverpool is the most 'film city' outside of London," Mulville said.

"It kind of makes sense that you have a state-of-the-art studio here.

"It's such a fabulous city to shoot in - the locations are brilliant.

"I've spoken to many producers who shoot locations here but then are forced to go down south to Pinewood and Shepperton to complete their production."

He added: "If this building was in London, it would have been redeveloped many, many years ago."
