articles.title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86
articles.summary: Stewart died in Los Angeles after living with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
articles.body:
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86.

Stewart died on Wednesday in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement on Thursday.

Although best known for his film and television roles, Stewart spent much of his career onstage, performing Shakespeare and other classics.

His career included performances as Claudius and Macbeth, a one-man adaptation of “A Christmas Carol”, and West End and Broadway productions of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” alongside longtime friend Ian McKellen.

Stewart earned some of the best reviews of his career for his 2007 portrayal of Macbeth, including his only Tony Award nomination. The Times of London described his Macbeth performance as “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour”.

“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told the Associated Press news agency in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”

From working-class Yorkshire to Shakespeare

Raised in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.

He joined an amateur drama group at 12 and, as a teenager, memorised Shakespeare for fun. A scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School helped launch his acting career.

Stewart, who developed alopecia at a young age, had been bald since he was 19.

His childhood was also marked by domestic violence. His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”

Stewart later became a patron of Refuge, a charity supporting survivors of domestic abuse.

Stewart spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, playing everyone from Mark Antony and Henry IV to Shylock and Oberon.

“People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?'” he told the AP. “Telly?”

He eventually left and appeared in the 1981 film “Excalibur”. In 1987, shortly after performing in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, he was offered a role in a science fiction series.

“I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail,” he said.

But “Star Trek: The Next Generation” ran for seven seasons and 178 episodes. Stewart became known worldwide as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, whose command, “Make it so”, became one of the show’s best-known lines.

Stewart also played Professor Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men, beginning with the 2000 film “X-Men”. He returned to the role in several sequels, including 2017’s “Logan”, alongside Hugh Jackman as Wolverine.

Stewart died just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series, which aired from 1966 to 1969.

Queen Elizabeth II knighted Stewart in June 2010. He also served as an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.

articles.summary: New Delhi: In an outburst sure to embarrass the govt, Supreme Court Thursday slammed the ministry of corporate affairs for “completely hijacking” the two
articles.body: New Delhi: In an outburst sure to embarrass the govt, Supreme Court Thursday slammed the ministry of corporate affairs for “completely hijacking” the two most important quasi-judicial financial adjudicatory bodies – National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the appellate NCLAT.The stinging remarks came from a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing petitioners who have been complaining for the last few months about the shoddy infrastructure, lack of support staff and large vacancies hampering the work in NCLT, which in the financial year 2024-25 had approved resolution plans worth Rs 55,000 crore. The tribunal adjudicates corporate civil disputes, company law violations and insolvency proceedings.“The system, the tribunals, we are compelled to observe, has been completely hijacked by the ministry of corporate affairs. That is the problem. And that is impinging on the autonomy of these institutions. These are the things we must look into. The ministry wants to have a complete whip over these tribunals. That is what is most unfortunate,” said the CJI.The bench has sought detailed proposals on infrastructure and staffing from the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT in four weeks.Contractual employees harassing judicial members, let past and present staff go: SCAppearing for NCLT Bar Association, senior advocate Sanjiv Sen said the roofs of certain floors in the building housing NCLT are collapsing and have become unusable. A large number of posts of judicial and technical members are lying vacant, he said, adding that the most unfortunate part is that out of 320 regular posts in NCLT, 253 are vacant.At this juncture, senior advocate Meenakshi Arora said the ministry has outsourced recruitment of contractual employees to a foreign firm and that could jeopardise the integrity of the important financial adjudicatory body. She said the existing contractual employees have already rendered service for eight years and must not be displaced.CJI Kant said, “We are not approving contractual recruitment of employees. It must be done through the Union Public Service Commission or Staff Selection Commission.” When Arora said termination of contractual employees must be stayed, the bench said, “We will not do any such thing at the behest of contractual staff. We would like to give full autonomy to the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT on this issue. The only thing is how soon it should happen.”The CJI said, “Contractual employment means backdoor entry. In Bombay for instance, I know how these contractual employees ran away with original files and FIRs had to be registered. They do not care about the judicial members or technical members. Some technical members are still manipulating certain things.”“But these contractual employees are harassing the judicial members. So let the past and present contractual employees go. Let the autonomy of recruitment be with the president of the tribunals.... The heads of these tribunals are the most suitable persons to assist us in suggesting ways and means to smoothen and strengthen the day-to-day functioning of these two important tribunals, including requirements of land and buildings and safekeep of records.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: What makes a golden eagle chick called Beaky Junior so important?
articles.summary: The bird's arrival on a managed grouse moor in southern Scotland is seen as a key moment for the species.
articles.body:
A golden eagle chick has become the first to fledge from a nest on a managed grouse moor in the south of Scotland.

The bird - Beaky Junior - hatched in a nest in a secret location in the Moffat Hills, at a site used for recreational gamebird shooting.

It comes after a Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) report revealed that two-thirds of UK persecution incidents involving birds of prey had occurred at similar sites.

And it is being considered a "hugely significant milestone" by those running a project to boost golden eagle numbers in the region.

Dr Cat Barlow, chief executive of Restoring Upland Nature (Run) which is behind the scheme, said they had received "incredible support" from landowners and gamekeepers.

The project to relocate birds from the Highlands to a secret location in the Moffat Hills started in the summer of 2018.

Numbers in the south of Scotland had fallen to a handful of breeding pairs but they are now at a record level of more than 50 - despite some setbacks.

Birds have been shot at or killed and that is why the birth of Beaky Junior - one of five golden eagle chicks successfully fledged in the area this year - is being seen as so significant, since it happened on a managed grouse moor.

Golden eagles flourish despite deaths and disappearances

Golden eagle released in conservation project shot with 17 pellets

It said they were widely scattered across the country but the majority - 64.3% - had occurred on land managed for gamebird shooting.

Against that backdrop, the efforts in southern Scotland to encourage estates and conservationists to work together are seen as particularly important.

Beaky Junior was even named by local gamekeepers in recognition of the "key role" they have played in helping golden eagles thrive.

Barlow explained: "It is wonderful to see a golden eagle hatch, fledge and fly freely from the newly-established nest of a translocated golden eagle that has made its home on a managed grouse moor in the Southern Uplands.

"This reflects the incredible support we have had from landowners and gamekeepers – from translocations in the Highlands, to continued monitoring and protection of birds and eyries on their lands and estates.

"Indeed their support has been absolutely vital to our success in restoring the population of golden eagles to record numbers."

She said the fledging of five chicks from the nests of birds they had translocated to southern Scotland was a "hugely significant milestone".

Barlow added that it gave "genuine hope" in the battle to reverse biodiversity decline and ensure future generations across Scotland, England and Wales could experience the "incredible sense of awe" when seeing a golden eagle.

Michael Clarke, who chairs Run, said individuals from "all walks of life" had helped the birds to thrive.

He added that they would continue to monitor the impact of the golden eagles on the area "with support of land managers, gamekeepers, farmers and the wider community".

The chief executive of landowner body Scottish Land and Estates, Sarah-Jane Laing, said it was thrilled to hear gamekeepers had named the chick.

"Beaky Junior's arrival serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved when land managers and conservationists unite behind a shared vision, grounded in trust and genuine partnership," she said.

"Seeing this magnificent species return to and flourish in these landscapes is something we can all take pride in."

The gamekeepers involved asked to remain anonymous in order to protect the location of the bird.

Speaking on their behalf, Mark Ewart, regional co-ordinator at the Southern Uplands Moorlands Group, added: "It is incredibly rewarding to see gamekeepers celebrated for the important role they have played in the success of Run's South of Scotland Golden Eagle Project.

"Monitoring and providing the right habitats for golden eagles and other species to flourish is an important part of what gamekeepers do on a day-to-day basis.

"To encounter golden eagles daily is the ultimate indicator of the success of the project-gamekeeper partnership."

articles.title: Scottish police to target online gangs forcing children to self-harm
articles.summary: Officers are hunting members of loose online networks of sadists who mainly targets girls on gaming platforms and social media.
articles.body:
Detectives in Scotland have joined international law enforcement in targeting online gangs which groom and coerce children into acts of self-harm.

Officers are hunting members of loose online networks of sadists known as "The Com", which mainly targets girls on gaming platforms and social media.

The groups, mostly comprised of teenage and young adult males, have risen in prominence in recent years after cases involving sextortion and hacking, as well as self-harm encouragement.

So far, there has been one arrest in Scotland, while there have been a handful of convictions in England.

The Molly Rose Foundation - a suicide prevention charity helping young people and families victimised by the network - said the groups "represent the gravest risk to children online".

Warning: This article contains distressing content

Gangs of teen boys target thousands of girls online

'My teenage daughter fell victim to a satanic online group – and I felt powerless to help'

Man who forced children to self-harm online jailed

Paul, not his real name, is a detective constable working in Police Scotland's internet investigations unit.

In a locked room at the force's Scottish Crime Campus, he is showing the BBC images on a computer sent to the team by the National Crime Agency (NCA).

Flagged by National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States, the material was eventually passed to Police Scotland and on to Paul's desk.

He now has the job of sifting through horrific images of abuse and injury in order to identify the victim, as well as the Scottish perpetrator.

"Unfortunately, we are getting a lot of self-harm imagery," he tells BBC News.

"There's nearly a thousand images in this particular case, and we need to go through every single one of those."

This case is linked to a Com group - a violent collective that uses mainstream social media platforms to manipulate and blackmail girls into harming and abusing themselves.

Often, the police say, this is done by the group for "kudos", or clout, from their peers.

On the screen, one image show a young girl's arm covered in blood. Another shows blood used to daub a symbol on to a bathroom wall.

Paul alleges the girl in the case was directed to harm herself by someone she met online - understood to be a young male in Scotland.

"Usually, it's a young girl in these particular cases," Craig said. "We're finding a lot of vulnerable young girls that are between 11 and 17.

"Unfortunately, we discover down the line that there are other vulnerabilities that [perpetrators] are exploiting."

Among the pictures are occult or Satanic sigils, a way for the abusers to appear "as extreme as possible", says Craig.

He continues: "It's very common, but I don't think they believe these Satanic things.

"With these particular groups anyway, it's about how extreme, how much exploitation can you inflict on an individual.

"It's about how much control you can get, up to the point that they're getting them to self-harm."

The Com - short for "the community" - are loosely-affiliated online groups involved in acts of abuse, financial crimes and extremism.

Groups involved in recent court cases include "The 764" and "CVLT". However, membership and group dynamics shift over time.

In May, the NCA said it was investigating around 200 cases involving these networks, while there have been a number of convictions.

In August, 20-year-old Justin Swaddle was jailed for two years for blackmailing and coercing more than 100 victims into acts of self-harm, including carving his online username on their bodies.

Det Ch Insp Craig Faulds - who leads efforts targeting groups' links to Scotland - described the crimes as "an evolution of online child abuse and sexual exploitation".

He told the BBC that often abusers will target their victims on "innocuous gaming platforms".

He continued: "It can move to social media platforms, messaging services and online forums.

"We are seeing cases where perpetrators online are targeting young vulnerable people, usually girls, and they are manipulating them, they are coercing them into sharing indecent images of themselves.

"Some of the more serious cases are seen by coercing individuals to cause acts of serious self-harm.

"We have identified victims and perpetrators in Scotland. And we are at the stage of mapping this threat to understand significance and the prevalence of it."

Hazel Stewart, who works for the NCA's Threat Leadership team, described the prevalence of Com groups are "low-volume, high-harm", adding: "The scale doesn't matter, it is the harm that is being caused."

She told the BBC that the abusers themselves are often young males who have been socially isolated or bullied.

"They find their own identity online, they can be whoever they want to be," she said.

"And therefore they are encouraging those that are vulnerable, usually young females... seeking them out, say, on suicidal ideation sites or eating disorder sites, and encourage them into more private spaces."

Stewart explained that abusers form relationships with victims and "be very supportive at first" before encouraging them to carry out harmful acts.

"It might be a small cut at first. Or it might be harm to a pet, or a sibling," she said.

"That harm will escalate and the grooming and manipulation continues, and the victim is in a situation where they can't escape."

Stewart described the threat as a "global problem" and said the UK was working with law enforcement in the USA, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, as well as Interpol and Europol.

The Molly Rose Foundation has recently warned about Com networks. Its chief executive Andy Burrows said it was "becoming the frontline of child protection online".

He said that online safety regulator Ofcom had been warned about the threat of online gangs and had been slow to respond - a "failure" that he said highlighted weaknesses in the Online Safety Act.

He continued: "These networks represent the gravest risk to children online, with every UK police force investigating Com cases, the threat is real and widespread.

"It's also clear that these risks exist beyond just social media, on gaming platforms and encrypted messaging apps, which is why Andy Burnham must move beyond a blanket social media ban and incentivise all online platforms to become safe for young people as a price of doing business in the UK."

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "The threats posed by Com groups are a particular concern for Ofcom, and we're working closely with law enforcement and child protection agencies to tackle them.

"Where services fail to comply with their duties, we've shown that we won't hesitate to act."

articles.title: Fired US general admits leaking classified Iran, Ukraine information to journalists: Report
articles.summary: The US Army general fired by defence secretary Pete Hegseth admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Iran and Ukraine to journalists
articles.body: The US Army general fired by defence secretary Pete Hegseth admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Iran and Ukraine to journalists over a period of roughly a year, according to an internal investigation report reviewed by Axios.Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, who headed the Joint Chiefs of Staff’s Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate, known as the J5, acknowledged sharing classified information with two reporters from separate media outlets, according to the report. A US official told Axios that Sylvia made the admissions on video after failing multiple polygraph tests during the investigation.Sylvia was dismissed by Hegseth on Wednesday over what the Pentagon described as severe misconduct. The investigation, which has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, remains ongoing.According to the report, the disclosures began as early as June 2025 and continued after the Pentagon tightened restrictions on media access. Sylvia allegedly communicated with reporters through the encrypted messaging application Signal and also met one journalist in person at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia.The report said the diner meeting took place after the journalist’s access to the Pentagon had been revoked. During the meeting, Sylvia relied on notes he had made while reviewing a classified report to orally share information about US assistance to Ukraine. The journalist was working on a book and met Sylvia twice, the report said. Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagon’s public affairs office or seek clearance before sharing the information.Investigation points to deleted messagesThe investigation also raised questions about Sylvia’s handling of communications with one of the reporters. According to the report, he received a Signal message sometime in June or July that he believed concerned Iran. Sylvia said he could not recall its precise contents and claimed he had deleted the message, believing he had accidentally erased the entire conversation thread. This also removed Signal messages and calls that could otherwise have been recovered from his personal phone.US officials suspect Sylvia deliberately deleted the communications and presented the action as accidental. The report also said he admitted to being one of 20 officials cited in a media story critical of Pentagon leadership.Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office had lobbied the Joint Staff to issue a statement supporting Sylvia in an effort to limit the damage from any future allegations of leaks. The Joint Staff later withdrew the statement after someone in the Defence Department informed it of the reasons behind Sylvia’s dismissal.US president Donald Trump, asked about the firing on Thursday, said Sylvia had “big problems” and that the administration was “very much looking for leakers”. Trump appeared to refer to Sylvia using female pronouns.Separately to the Axios report, a defence department official also confirmed to Al Jazeera that Sylvia was under investigation for leaking classified information concerning the Iran war, Russia’s war against Ukraine and other matters. The official said he had failed three polygraph tests and accused him of putting national security at risk. The official also stressed that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, saying that responsibility rested with Centcom and its commander, Adm Brad Cooper.Hegseth’s wider crackdown on leaksSylvia’s dismissal is the latest action in Hegseth’s campaign against unauthorised disclosures to the media. In July, the Pentagon announced a joint task force with the Justice Department to identify leakers and directed its Office of General Counsel to prioritise prosecutions over the unauthorised release of classified information.The Pentagon had also introduced restrictive rules governing journalists’ access and reporting in October 2025, prompting several news organisations and defence reporters to surrender their press credentials.Sylvia is the second officer to be removed from the J5 position under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt Gen Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement in October last year.No immediate replacement has been named for Sylvia, according to an official cited by The Associated Press.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mushroom killer to be jailed for life after appeals court finds sentence too light
articles.summary: An attempt by murderer Erin Patterson, who killed three people with a meal of toxic mushrooms, to overturn her conviction has failed, with an appeals court finding that her original sentence was too light.
articles.body: An attempt by murderer Erin Patterson, who killed three people with a meal of toxic mushrooms, to overturn her conviction has failed, with an appeals court finding that her original sentence was too light for her “cold and calculated” crimes. Patterson, now 52, was found guilty last July after a jury trial that attracted international attention due to the unusual method of murder – death cap mushrooms hidden inside portions of beef wellington at a family lunch in July 2023. The Australian mother was given three life sentences for the murder of three people, including her estranged husband’s parents, as well as 25 years for the attempted murder of a fourth guest, the local pastor, who recovered after weeks in hospital. She was sentenced to a non-parole period of 33 years, meaning she would have been in her 80s when freed. However, three appeals court judges instead found Friday that her crimes – which included an “elaborate series of deceptions” – were so “extraordinarily cold and calculated” that she deserved to be in prison for life. “In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period,” said Justice Stephen McLeish. Patterson’s lawyers had presented seven grounds of appeal in the hope that the mother of two would be granted a retrial. On the first ground, they took issue with the way the jury members were sequestered, which they claimed was “catastrophic” to their case. During the trial, held in the small Victorian town of Morwell, jury members shared a hotel at various times with prosecutors and witnesses. While there was no evidence that the guests interacted, Patterson’s lawyers said the possibility of interactions “cannot be excluded.” However, the three appeals court judges found “there was no objective basis for a fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function of rendering a verdict according to law.” The judges also rejected suggestions that some evidence shouldn’t have been submitted, including cellphone data that put Patterson near the location of death cap mushrooms posted to a citizen scientist website. The judges found the evidence was admissible as part of the prosecution’s “wider circumstantial case.” This is a developing story. More to come.

articles.title: A Michigan father and his family have added a pirate ship to their front-yard Halloween world, complete with blue lighting and skeleton sailors, with live actors set to take over on October 31
articles.summary: Across Sterling Heights, Michigan, Halloween is more than a night of costumes and candy.
articles.body: Across Sterling Heights, Michigan, Halloween is more than a night of costumes and candy. It is a season of elaborate transformations, when ordinary front yards become haunted graveyards, mythical creatures emerge from the shadows, and homeowners turn their properties into miniature horror attractions. According to the City of Sterling Heights, a growing community of residents is keeping the tradition alive through imaginative displays that bring neighbors together and give trick-or-treaters something extraordinary to remember.A pirate ship sets sailFor Nathan Robinson and his family, Halloween decorating has evolved into an elaborate storytelling exercise. "Their latest is a pirate ship, lit in deep blue, ringed by skeletal sailors, and meant to call to mind a ship going down to a supernatural watery grave." Nearby, creepy clowns add another layer of unease to the unfolding scene.The Sterling Heights residents, who have been building their displays for years, approach the yard as a carefully planned experience. According to the City of Sterling Heights, Robinson maps out how visitors should move through the installation, deciding what they should see and feel at each stage.His wife and five children contribute to the process, from planning and construction to sharing videos of the finished spectacle. On October 31, the family will take the experience further by welcoming relatives from out of town to help bring the display to life with live actors.Neighbourhoods built on frightRobinson is part of a wider community of Sterling Heights residents who dedicate substantial time and creativity to Halloween. On Hanson Avenue, Rick and Kathy Stys have been transforming their property since 2010. What began as a modest cemetery has grown into a collection of skeletons, themed installations and custom props. In 2024, they won the Beautification Commission's Halloween contest.This year's ghost-themed display continues a tradition of keeping visitors guessing. The couple begins its Halloween countdown as early as July, reflecting a commitment that extends well beyond the final week of October.Monsters, gargoyles and handmade horrorsElsewhere, Paul Nesterowich's corner property features a formidable gargoyle weighing approximately 500 pounds, with a wingspan of 14 feet. The animated creature growls and spreads its wings, while dozens of spiders, headless horsemen and other figures complete the scene. The City of Sterling Heights reports that assembling the display takes at least 60 hours.On Canal Drive, Randy and Kristy Watycha combine commercial props with handmade creations. Their collection includes Beulah, a vintage Halloween figure dating to the 1950s, alongside customised skeletons and sensor-triggered scares.Tyrus and Melissa Napier have also built a neighbourhood favourite since 2019, featuring a crashed UFO, horror-film-inspired scenes and a haunted graveyard. Tyrus gives pirate buffs decorating tips and sells used props at their latest show.More than a Halloween displayBeyond the elaborate creatures and theatrical lighting, these yards represent a shared neighbourhood tradition. According to the City of Sterling Heights, residents exchange ideas, help one another build props and inspire more households to decorate. articles.title: The Traitors: Bombshell confession as faithfuls finally turn the screw
articles.summary: Could the faithfuls finally come good in Thursday's penultimate episode?
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

With the traitors still riding high following last Friday's episode, could they really just walk it to the final? It was time to find out.

Having been bestowed with the almighty power of the double dagger - well, metaphorically speaking, at least - King Kenny held all the cards, choosing to use his special power of a double vote to send another faithful packing.

As cliffhangers go, it wasn't hugely thrilling for viewers at home, given that the pair up for banishment - Sharon Rooney and Joanne McNally - were both faithfuls.

Nevertheless, it left a big impact on the faithful crew as they realised they had let the traitors land yet another blow ahead of Friday's final.

"We've got to pull something out of the bag," said frustrated faithful Michael Sheen later. He wasn't wrong.

Joanne got teary as she departed and joked "she was premenstrual," before revealing she was "a hardcore faithful".

Maya described her as a "ball of fun", while Kenny put on his best acting skills in the aftermath by pretending to be struggling with having the deciding vote, even comforting poor Sharon. Give that man an Oscar.

Meanwhile, James Blunt was on the hunt for whiskey like a teenager at the end of a house party: "Where do they keep the stiff stuff?" he asked himself, finding only a tray of empty glasses.

Murder was soon on the minds of the traitors again as the dastardly trio of Kenny, Maya and James A trudged up to the turret.

"The life of a traitor... it's not for everyone," said Maya. And that probably includes James A, although to be fair, he has shown a bit more enthusiasm for some pantomime villainy in the last couple of episodes. More on him later.

"Let's have faith," said King Kenny without a hint of irony.

As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.

When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."

Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.

Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.

Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.

And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.

Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."

She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.

On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"

James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.

This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.

Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.

"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.

Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.

Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.

And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).

Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."

In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.

Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.

The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.

Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.

Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.

James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"

At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.

And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DSI Sheen is on her case.

articles.title: France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
articles.summary: Authorities vow firm action against violence as yellow vest and student movements announce widespread demonstrations.
articles.body:
France’s interior minister has announced the deployment of 70,000 police officers across the country in preparation for planned protests on Saturday, coinciding with Halloween.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Thursday that security measures, including the use of armoured vehicles and water cannon introduced last week , will be strengthened.

Nationwide protests over the rising cost of living have rocked France, with some degenerating into large-scale looting and riots.

“The day of October 31 presents a very high risk of public disorder,” Nunez said at a news conference.

About 70,000 police officers and gendarmes will be mobilised, matching the number deployed at last week’s protests, he said, calling the move an “exceptional measure”.

Demonstrations last Saturday drew about 410,000 protesters nationwide, according to the interior ministry, though unions put the figure at roughly double that. The ministry said more than 2,700 people were arrested a week earlier.

The “ yellow vest ” movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday.

Nunez warned demonstrators against using Halloween as “a legitimate reason to hide one’s face” to cause disturbances in public areas.

He told reporters demonstrations would be allowed, but “not in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.

The interior minister issued a warning to far-right groups that clashed with left-wing protesters at rallies in about 15 French cities.

“We will tolerate no excesses,” he said, and pledged an “extremely firm” response.

Nunez accused the “ultra-left” movement and some yellow vest activists of circulating messages on social media promoting demonstrations on Halloween evening that called for a “revolution”.

“These gatherings will be banned,” he said.

The yellow vest movement has already announced a “third act” of its protests on Halloween and called for demonstrations outside the National Assembly and all town halls in the country.
